stances.claim: Aguirre ear-cupping constituted direct contempt (done in open court) punishable summarily; the defense team press conference constituted indirect contempt (done outside court) requiring formal charge and hearing -- though Roy instant acceptance rendered due process moot.

The plain admonition imposed on Aguirre was not even a penalty under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court -- creating the practical irony of too much ado about nothing in terms of actual sanctions despite the televised drama.
stances.rhetorical_move: technical-sanction-inadequacy observation (plain admonition is not a penalty)

stances.claim: Contempt should be invoked judiciously and sparingly, especially when free expression is involved; courts should set an example of dignified restraint rather than muzzling critics -- following the 1918 US v. Bustos wisdom that a clear conscience, not muzzled critics, is the balm for wounds.

notable_anecdotes: Aguirre packing his clothes in preparation for an expected heavier sanction of detention -- only to be merely admonished within 2-3 minutes of a caucus that lasted less time than the drama it produced.
Roy gallant acceptance of the reprimand: I thank the impeachment court that the other defense lawyers were not included -- transforming a punitive moment into a display of collegial chivalry.

The UP Faculty contempt case (2008): the Supreme Court merely admonished law professors for their public statement criticizing an SC decision -- used to establish that even the highest court should not muzzle critics.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers readers' question of whether the Corona impeachment trial's two contempt proceedings were 'too much ado about nothing.' Vitaliano Aguirre II was cited for cupping his ears while Sen. Santiago was rebuking the prosecution -- a 'galactic act of epal' in Santiago's words, done in open court (direct contempt, punishable summarily); the Senate resolved to merely admonish him within 2-3 minutes of a caucus, though Aguirre was caught on camera packing his clothes for an expected detention. The entire defense team (except retired Justice Cuevas) was cited for a press conference claiming Malacañang offered senators P100 million each in soft projects -- done outside the court (indirect contempt, requiring formal written charge and hearing); none could name their source; only Jose Roy III was punished, with a reprimand, which he gallantly accepted: 'I thank the impeachment court that [the other defense lawyers] were not included in the penalty.' CJ clarifies that plain admonition is not even a penalty under Rule 140 (Re: Vasquez, 2008) -- making the Aguirre sanction technically nothing. When the source of contempt is protected free expression, courts must be cautious: citing the UP Faculty contempt case (2008, J. de Castro: 'All the Court demands is the same respect and courtesy that one lawyer owes to another') and the 1918 US v. Bustos wisdom that 'a clear conscience, not muzzled critics, is the balm for wounds.' CJ recommends that contempt be invoked judiciously and sparingly, and that courts set an example of dignified restraint.
